title: The question you see every day.
author: Jd-Phoenix
selftext:
Seriously, can I make a game using Ai purely? What I need to add to make a good game. I'm not talking slop, I'm talking actually functioning game. What do I need to learn and add to AI working.

I'm not underestimating how much work it requires to build a game. My problem is that I absolutely hate coding with passion. Like I just hate everything about it. I tried to bypass this hate and learn it but failed. The past few years I've been working on myself and learning new skills outside of gaming. But every time I go back to learning coding, I just hate my life. That's my problem. I tried to build a team where I help with directing, take care of narrative, testing, and music. Basically, everything but coding. I got rejected hard, made fun of, and attacked. It was horrible. I truly wanted to work with others, but found out, my only option to ever have a game is to wait until Ai is capable, or somehow I meet someone who isn't full of themselves.

comments.author: QuayDropEmOff
comments.body: ofc you can. just work in iterations. it’s not a one prompt and done process. just work on systems at a time and a lot of play testing. and if you can handle the art yourself that’s even better

comments.author: MaxwellHowl
comments.body:
Yes. You should research how games are made. Use the actual methods of game development. Have a GDD. Do a prototype. Playtest. Iterate. Playtest. Iterate. Alpha. Beta. 1.0

You can literally have Claude explain the process to you and help you through it.

Don't just say "Claude make this game".

Write your idea/gimmick down, stick to it. You don’t need one if you’re the only person.

It’s good to help make pitching to publishers easier though.

comments.author: Halloween_Forever_
comments.body: With absolutely no coding? You'll need a budget. Create agents to review, and retask what fails review. Port your engine, AI service, and project tools into one gui that has dedicated shared folders. It's going to take work and time to go back and fix what needs fixing. Try to do everything in short steps. If you rush it you may waste days going back and trying to make what went wrong, right. Just to find out you need to change the direction of the design.

comments.author: Razrie
comments.body:
I have a game that just hit update 600, and it is not even a full first stage of the game, and im still nowhere near happy enough with the game to move on to the next stage.  Get a plan for a playable first version with minimum content and graphics.  Run through it and make a list of things that you want to behave in different ways.  

An example I came up with "feel sliders"  these have core mechanics, like timing windows, enemy aggression, stamina recovery, damage dealt.  With a copy settings button.  Then run through the game and tweak them when things dont feel good.  The game wont know it.  It's up to you. 

I spent about 10 hours of testing time on wolves.   Now they circle you to attack, fake you out, take turns attacking, dodge your heavy attacks.  Behave differently when there are different numbers of wolves.  

I literally started having trouble winning against them at one point, and not because of just damage numbers being too high.

comments.author: drizzkek
comments.body:
Absolutely, you can build just about anything with AI. Whether or not it’s slop isn’t a byproduct of using AI, it’s related more so to your process and ability to deliver results using the AI tools.

There’s a few layers to this. You can decide early on if you want to use AI generated assets, or take the approach of building entire procedurally generated stages with snow and rain and rocks and trees using nothing but mathematics. It’s possible to make a game that uses nothing AI generated assets, only AI assisted development.

But, take a step back. AI development is about harnessing the power of AI so you feed it the ideas, and work with it to get the results you want, all while asking it to make that some written process a long the way so that you don’t repeat the same mistakes. If you don’t like the way it did something, don’t blame the AI, go talk to it. Ask it how can we get the result you’re wanting, how to “close the gaps” why it wasn’t what you imagined.

If you work with it long enough and fully embrace that it needs you as much as you need it, your project will grow, and your results will start shaping into what you’re imagining. You are a partner, you must be hands on loading up that game world and checking the result. And building a development workflow that gives Claude, for example, the ability to self heal the world, and the tools to “see” the world. It isn’t some magical “it knows how to make a perfect game”. What it lacks is process and a pilot, which is you.

I’ve spent about 6 months developing a game, and at this point Claude runs 24/7 working a queue of tickets. It utilizes test driven development, uses in game clients, headless clients, all sorts of tools and processes I have created so that it works autonomously. It’s possible to build whatever you want, but you’ve got to understand it’s a lot of work. It’s not easy by any means, but it sure is fun.

comments.author: ZeusGameAssets
comments.body:
I'm sorry you had such a bad experience trying to learn programming. You have to dissociate that with actual programming and have a different perspective on each.

Programming is actually about having 100% control over everything that happens in your game. Even the best AI models can't replicate that level of control, because you're communicating using natural language, and there are a lot of layers of errors, interpretations, decisions, contexts, that prevent you from accurately describing what you want. So you end up babysitting the AI, and when your project gets bigger, every new prompt can fix a problem and create 10.

I'm not saying you'll have to learn everything about programming, but knowing enough to effectively direct agents is a skill that will help you make better games.

Before knowing how to program, I had these airy-fairy ideas that were very unrealistic, learning to program helped me ground my game ideas and have a more realistic perspective over what can be accomplished and the costs involved. Every decision you make or delegate to an AI agent will have consequences on the complexity of your project, its performance and maintainability, and if you accumulate too many bad decisions, even the most powerful agent will have a hard time navigating your project and adding new features, or fixing the existing ones, it will become increasingly more expensive in token use versus being proactive in how you guide your agents into making a nice piece of software.

Your growth is hiding behind the challenges that are going to require the most emotional labour from you. But the bright side is: programming is incredibly fun and addictive once you get past the beginner stage, it'd be a shame to let your past experiences prevent you from feeling the waves of raw pleasure that you feel when you're 3 hours deep into the code and everything clicks. And when you use AI agents as your own dev team it gets even better because you can delegate the boring stuff and do the fun parts yourself.

comments.author: LCRGaming
comments.body:
Give it your idea and it'll save the concept so you can always come back to it and it will ensure the agent stays on target. Create a repository so you can iterate without worrying about overwriting everything and not being able to backtrack when something fails miserably, because it will. Commit each feature, update, or bug fix after it's done, don't let long sessions with multiple features sit uncommitted. Once you get started you can iterate all day and continue to make progress mainly small batches at a time until you get to something playable. Once you have a good prototype, find the things that are missing. Sounds, animation, music, models, etc. and start to fill in those gaps. I like to make todo notes as I play and then add them to a [todo.md](http://todo.md) so I can get the AI to organize them, and fix them in smaller batches. This is the basics for most of my games I've built even before I started building with AI. 

The hard part is the idea and style/taste. I copied games in my early days just to see what the process might be. That was in the 90s and I'd copy tank games, skater games, etc. until I understood how they might work, I read a lot too about game theory which can never hurt, even today. 

With AI, once you get a good workflow going you'll see your progress start to improve and move faster. You'll have an idea and see it take shape in an afternoon and know if it's something you want to pursue or not. Regardless, don't throw it away even if you think it's something you won't continue with, keep it, you never know when you might come back to it and go "oh, what's why it sucked" and start it up again. I've done that with game ideas I've sat on for 15 years just recently. Hope that helps.

comments.author: That-Drink5946
comments.body:
Here you go I was writing this down a bit for myself but then realized I could write it down for you here:

Best advice is to ignore the advice from "content creators", they really have no insight, well most of them.

What you could study is game architecture and sensible things to think of during development.

You can actually get these answers from your LLM by just asking it.

Essentially this is what I would do today (and are doing actually):

I would make sure the LLM knows the basic setup of my environment.
This means:
Learn Git. Git is a revision system. And you really need to know or at least be able to have discussions with your LLM about it.
With a revision system you can go back when things are added that break things.
A revision system allows you to view changes between "versions" of files. One file can change many times and you can track each change there. Allowing you to have full control over the code that is generated. Or rather, your LLM can have full control.

Second, make sure the LLM adds plenty of tests to verify that your code is not containing issues that will pop up later, or to simply verify that things actually works. LLMs are super good at testing, but make sure you tell your LLM to add enough tests so that you have a good "coverage", just say 90 % coverage if you need.

Pick a language. I don't know if you have a preferred one, find one.
My preferred language is Odin. Because it is just fulfilling all the things I want out of a language.

Here's another advice you may not hear:
Prefer to build it on your own, especially the UI's.
Tell your LLM to build your own UI library. Study UI libraries and learn how they work. What variants there are. Then pick the one you like.
Do not use the existing UI's like Qt, WxWidgets or other crap like that. Those all look like they belong in the 70s. If you make your own UI chances are you will get exactly what you want.

This UI library you can then use in all your "products".
Making people recognize your products.

Don't go with OpenGL today. It's old. Go with Vulkan on Windows or Linux, on Mac Metal.
This is why I like Odin which have amazing support for all of these.

Today when you do a game, you do not want to put heavy stuff on the CPU as much as in GPU.
This is typical AAA thinking. If you can, put it on the GPU.
Never put heavy stuff on the main thread. Your input go on that thread and you will suffer with lag, missed frames or jerkiness. Use asynchronous threads utilizing your cores here.

Tell your LLM to always try to use SIMD instructions when it can as well.

For audio ask your LLM to find a good 3rd party library or do what I did, and tell your LLM to build your own audio library.

Now after all these basics, you need to give it your ideas. And here you can write as much as you like and tell your LLM to use any tools you want.
It is just a world of possibilities out there.
I have my own setup here for managing tasks, there are plenty of these out there.

One thing though, don't build the game. Build the editor, that you can switch into the game with. I would have that as one of the more important points in designing the game.

For example make your tab key instantly toggle between in game mode and in game but in edit mode. For example.

Try to explain as much as you can about the game. Then build the implementation plan and the tickets. But put the editor details in there also.
Start smaller here. Quick iterations is far better than large.

Go over the implementation plan, add stuff. You can do this for a long time.
But then before you start, make sure to tell your AI to create frequent milestones, so that you can verify the work.

Also and I almost forgot, tell it to do mockups. If you have a new feature you want in, that will be visible, tell it to do 3 variations of mockups for you, as a rule you tell it to always create mockups when you have user facing features.
This is also where that UI can come in handy as you can get it to create mockups for you with the actual UI.
 
I also enforce a rule that it has to think about complimentary colors always when drawing fonts. I never want to see a white font on a bright yellow background for example. There are exact calculations you can do to always be as visible as possible.
But do avoid the full white full black text. It causes eyestrain. Use pearl and ebony instead.

For me I never ever use normal fonts. Normal fonts are slow and ugly. This is a typical beginner thing to not realize. Any AAA game today or editor are using MTSDF fonts, or signed distance field fonts. Essentially think SVG on GPU. Fast and smooth in any size. https://github.com/chlumsky/msdfgen

There's a lot more to say here, but you know.. just ask the LLM.

Finally I could expand on the Git comment I did above. I actually don't use git directly, I use Jijutsu https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj, which is much better for LLMs. But this sits on-top of Git. It avoids agents from wrecking each others work.

AI could make you a great game, that’s less a problem. But once you launch it and get real players and you need to maintain it then it is a different story, because you have to know what changes since last version and would that break the current experience or expectations of your customers that already bought your game.

comments.author: hydroxyHU
comments.body:
I think the most important thing is to play your own game a lot—and other games, too.

Don’t just rush through your own game. Take your time and play at a slower pace, letting the mechanics sink in and making you rethink your design decisions. Here’s what I mean: Do you really need that extra prompt? Is this really the best way to achieve what you’re trying to do?

AI can write code, but it can’t experience your game the way you do. The “juice” is incredibly important: microanimations, sound effects, and all those little details. For example, when you hover over a button, it should give you subtle feedback. When you click it, there should be a clear visual indication that something happened.

It’s also important to understand your individual subsystems and the rules behind them. AI can code incredibly fast, but if you don’t keep a close eye on it, things can go wrong very quickly. Sometimes remnants of old functionality are left behind, and the AI starts layering new code on top of them. Before you know it, you have no idea why something isn’t working—or why it’s behaving differently than you intended.

Sometimes the AI will skip parts of the implementation, too, and your game ends up becoming a patchwork of half-working systems if you’re not paying close attention.

Unfortunately, I had to learn this the hard way.

I spent two months working on a more complex medieval castle-defense game inspired by Frostpunk’s morale and decision-making systems. Eventually, I realized that I no longer understood how the underlying systems worked, despite all the documentation and planning.

Planning and prototyping are absolutely essential before tackling a larger project. With smaller games, you can get away with improvising a bit more.

comments.author: richchiudev
comments.body:
>First, I’m really sorry you got mocked for trying to build a team. People online love to dunk on "non-coders," even though directing, narrative, music, and rigorous testing are massive parts of making a game actually good.  
To answer your question honestly: **Yes, you can build a genuinely functioning, good game with AI without writing code yourself—but you have to become a really good "Technical Director."**  
I think here is what you actually need to bring to the table so it doesn't turn into "slop":Pick a friendly engine like Godot, start small, and treat AI as your junior programmer while you act as the director. You don't need anyone's permission to start!

comments.author: imlo2
comments.body:
Coding is just a way (although a very difficult one) to express what kind of behavior you want to make to a game, tool or whatever it might be. So if you now have AI in use, you don't have to "code", but logical thinking, decision-making and taste are equally important, perhaps much more so right now, since you don't need to spend weeks on algorithm implementations, reading APIs, etc. but focus on the idea and execution.

So if skipping coding on your part means you don't want to put effort into logical structure how your game works, and you want to offload it to someone else, then it's probably going to be quite difficult to make something solo. And if you need someone else, you should then work on that part, what makes you valuable to someone else, not just words, but show it.
